text: Lesson 18 produced a go-live checklist, a rollback plan, and an Architecture Decision Record -- written for the people who'll build and maintain this capability. Meridian's board is a different audience entirely. A hospital system CFO and a Lakeshore administrator don't need to know what a Script Include is. They need to decide whether St. Catherine's pilot earned the green light to roll this out to Lakeshore and Prairie View next.

A presentation that opens with 'we chose a scheduled pull over a webhook' has already lost the room. It opens instead with the outcome: one Service Desk, live in pilot, respecting every domain boundary the board already approved, on a four-to-five-month timeline inside their eighteen-month window. Only after that lands does each decision get named -- as a tradeoff resolved, in a sentence a board can actually evaluate, not a technical fact recited at them.

The ADR's own structure survives the translation almost exactly, with the vocabulary swapped. 'No webhook capability' becomes 'their system can't notify us when something changes.' The three options become 'force a new build under deadline pressure, check on a schedule, or run it by hand.' The decision becomes 'we check every fifteen minutes.' The consequence becomes 'that's acceptable for a help desk -- it would not be acceptable for payroll.' The reasoning never changes, only the words carrying it.

All three of Lesson 13's worried stakeholders are sitting in this same room, and each one needs their specific concern addressed by name. St. Catherine's hears that its detailed categories survived as subcategories, nothing flattened. Lakeshore hears it still controls its own subcategory list after launch. Prairie View hears the sentence that matters most to them: their legacy process stays live until their own go-live is confirmed, and they pilot last on purpose -- not because anyone forgot them, but because they asked for a say in the sequence.

Naming each concern inside one presentation is what lets this work for three very different audiences without three separate decks. The board nods on the outcome. But a presentation only survives a friendly room -- the next lesson puts these same decisions in front of a panel built to push back, the way a real CTA review would, on the specific choices this capstone actually made.
